common_name: Cuzco Gigante Corn (Peruvian Giant Choclo Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost; this high-altitude Sacred Valley landrace wants a long, cool-night growing season and performs best where summers are not scorching.

directions: Sow directly in deep, fertile soil once the ground has warmed, spacing plants generously since Cuzco Gigante grows into one of the tallest corn landraces in cultivation, often exceeding ten feet with ears carrying unusually large, starchy kernels. It is the classic corn used in Peru for 'choclo,' boiled on the cob and served with fresh cheese and ají, picked for eating fresh at the milky stage rather than left to fully dry like a field corn. Give it consistent moisture through tasseling and ear fill, and hill or stake stalks in windy sites since the tall canes can lodge. Harvest at peak milk stage for table use, or let ears dry fully on the stalk if saving seed or storing kernels.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

common_name: Kculli Corn (Maíz Morado, Peruvian Purple Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Kculli is among the oldest documented Andean corn races and is grown for its deep purple-black kernels and cob tissue.

directions: Sow in full sun once soil has warmed, grouping blocks of plants rather than single rows since corn is wind pollinated and isolation from other corn preserves the deep anthocyanin pigmentation in the kernels. Kculli, better known commercially as maíz morado or Peruvian purple corn, is harvested fully dry and the kernels and cobs are boiled down to make the dark purple base for chicha morada and mazamorra morada, two of Peru's best-known purple corn preparations. Let ears dry completely in the husk before shelling, and store kernels (with some cob fragments, which carry much of the pigment) in a cool, dry place. This landrace is one of the pigments-richest corns used in Andean anthocyanin research.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; this highland landrace is grown through to full dry maturity rather than harvested green.

directions: Grow exactly like other dry field corn, direct sown after soil warms and left on the stalk until husks and kernels are fully dry and hard. Confite Morocho is the traditional small, flinty-kerneled Andean race toasted in a hot skillet or oven to make 'cancha' (also called cancha serrana or corn nuts), a crunchy snack and common garnish for Peruvian ceviche and soups. Shell and store dried kernels in a sealed container; to prepare cancha, toast kernels in a dry pan or with a touch of oil until they pop open and turn golden and crisp. Its hard, low-moisture kernel is what allows it to toast rather than scorch the way softer sweet corn kernels do.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; isolate from other corn varieties if saving seed, since this landrace is prized specifically for its naturally sweet, translucent kernel.

directions: Sow directly in warm soil in full sun and keep evenly watered through tasseling and ear fill. Chullpi is an Andean landrace valued for kernels that stay naturally sweet and glassy-translucent, unlike the starchy field-corn types grown alongside it in the highlands, and it is traditionally eaten fresh off the cob or fermented into chicha de jora. Note that this maize landrace shares its name with an unrelated quinoa landrace of the same name grown in the same region — the two are different crops distinguished by scientific name. Harvest at the milk-to-early-dough stage for fresh eating, or let a portion dry fully on the stalk for seed saving or chicha brewing.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; like other Peruvian highland maize races, Paro tolerates the cool nights of mid-elevation Andean valleys better than lowland tropical corn types.

directions: Grow as a standard dry field corn, direct sown in full sun and left to mature fully on the stalk before harvest. Paro is one of the soft, starchy flour-type maize races documented among Peru's highland corn landraces, with kernels that grind easily once dried, traditionally parched or ground into meal for soups and breads rather than eaten fresh. Dry ears thoroughly on the stalk or under cover before shelling, and store cleaned kernels in a sealed, rodent-proof container. Because it is an open-pollinated highland landrace rather than a modern hybrid, expect more variability in ear size and kernel color between individual plants than with commercial corn.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; this central-highland Peruvian landrace needs a long frost-free season to fill its large kernels fully.

directions: Sow in deep, fertile soil in full sun and allow a long season for the large, starchy kernels to fully develop and dry on the stalk. Huayleño is a traditional landrace from the central Peruvian highlands grown for its big, soft kernels, which are soaked and boiled whole into mote, a staple cooked-corn side dish served throughout Andean Peru alongside stews, cheese, and roasted meats. Dry ears fully before shelling and store kernels in a cool, dry, sealed container; dried kernels are typically soaked overnight before the long simmer that softens them for mote. As an open-pollinated landrace it shows more natural variation in ear size than modern hybrid field corn.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)
